subject: Religionskunskap
title: Religion and society
sourceSummary: Freedom of religion and what it means in Sweden, secularisation and religion's place in society, the relationship between state and church up to the separation in the year 2000, religion's role in both conflict and peace work, and prejudice and religious diversity in Sweden today.
topics: religion in conflict and peace work

questions.prompt: What does freedom of religion mean in Sweden?
questions.opener: The freedom has both a positive and a negative side — think about both.
choices: That everyone living in Sweden must belong to some faith community
That only the five largest world religions are allowed in the country
That everyone has the right, alone or together with others, to practise their religion — and also the right to stand outside all religions
That religious rules take precedence over Swedish law for someone who is a believer
questions.explanation: Freedom of religion is protected in the Instrument of Government, one of Sweden's fundamental laws, and also in the European Convention and the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It has a positive side — the right to believe, practise and change religion — and a negative side, the right to stand entirely outside. The freedom is not, however, unlimited: Swedish law applies equally to everyone, and an act does not become permitted just because it is religiously motivated, which makes the last option wrong.

questions.opener: The word describes a change in religion's role — not a ban.
choices: That religion takes on a less prominent role in society and in many people's everyday lives, and that religion and politics are kept separate
That a religion is banned by law
That all inhabitants of a country switch to the same religion
That the state builds more churches and mosques
questions.explanation: Secularisation means that religion's influence declines over society's institutions, such as schools, healthcare and politics, and for many people also in their own lives. In international surveys, Sweden is usually counted as one of the world's most secularised countries, while at the same time many people are still members of faith communities and religious diversity has increased. Secularisation therefore does not mean that religion is banned — such a ban would, on the contrary, be a violation of freedom of religion.

questions.prompt: What happened to the relationship between the state and the Church of Sweden in the year 2000?
questions.opener: A relationship of several hundred years ended at the turn of the millennium.
choices: The Church of Sweden became the state church and took over responsibility for civil registration
The Church of Sweden was separated from the state and became one faith community among others, even though it is still regulated by a special law
All churches in Sweden were closed and activities moved into homes
Sweden introduced Catholicism as a new state religion
questions.explanation: On 1 January 2000, the Church of Sweden ceased to be the state church. Membership since then does not automatically follow from birth but is based on baptism or an individual choice, the church fee is no longer a tax, and responsibility for civil registration had already been moved to the state in 1991. The Church of Sweden is still Sweden's largest faith community and is regulated by a special law on the Church of Sweden, but in terms of freedom of religion it has the same standing as other communities. No new state religion was thus introduced.

questions.topic: religion in conflict and peace work
questions.prompt: Which statement about religion's role in conflicts is most accurate?
questions.opener: Think about whether religion is the only cause — and about what religious actors also do.
choices: All wars in the world are caused by religion
Religion never has anything to do with armed conflicts

Religion can be used to motivate and reinforce conflicts, but conflicts usually have several causes such as power, land and economics — and religious leaders and organisations also often work for reconciliation and peace
Under international law, religious organisations are not allowed to take part in peace work
questions.explanation: Conflicts called religious almost always have mixed causes: struggles over power, territory, resources and identity, where religion can become a group marker or a way of justifying violence. At the same time, religious actors have played important roles in peace work, for example through mediation, aid work and reconciliation processes, and interfaith dialogue is used as a method for reducing tensions. Both the first and the second options are thus too categorical and miss the more nuanced picture.

questions.opener: The word contains "pre" — something that comes before.
choices: A conclusion reached after carefully examining the facts
A law that protects minorities against discrimination
Another word for freedom of religion
A preconceived view of a person or group, held before you know anything about them
questions.explanation: A prejudice is a view formed in advance, without grounding in knowledge or personal experience. Prejudices can lead to discrimination and to hate crimes directed at, for example, Muslims (Islamophobia), Jews (antisemitism) or Christians, and they often rest on generalisations in which an entire group is attributed the same characteristics. Knowledge, personal encounters and the habit of examining one's own generalisations reduce prejudice. A prejudice is thus the exact opposite of a well-founded conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which statement about religious diversity in Sweden today is correct?
questions.opener: Think about how immigration and secularisation have interacted.
choices: In Sweden today, many different religions and world views exist side by side, while a large share of the population does not see itself as religiously believing
Everyone living in Sweden belongs to the Church of Sweden
Only Christian communities are allowed to operate in Sweden
Religious minorities lack legal protection in Sweden
questions.explanation: Through immigration and globalisation, Islam, Orthodox Christianity, Catholicism, Judaism, Buddhism and Hinduism, among others, are now represented in Sweden alongside the Church of Sweden and the free churches — while at the same time many people are non-believers or identify as, for example, secular humanists. Religious minorities are, moreover, protected by freedom of religion in the constitution and by the Discrimination Act, where religion or other belief is one of the grounds of discrimination, which makes the last option wrong.

questions.prompt: Explain step by step how Sweden went from being a country with a single permitted church to today's freedom of religion and religious diversity.
questions.opener: Follow the timeline from the Reformation up to today, and note what each step made possible.
questions.answer: After the Reformation in the 16th century, Sweden became an Evangelical Lutheran realm, and at the Uppsala Synod of 1593 it was established that the country should have a single doctrine. For a long time, all inhabitants were obliged to belong to the state church, and leaving it or spreading a different doctrine could be punished. During the 18th and 19th centuries the first exceptions appeared: immigrant groups gained certain rights, and in 1774–1775 Aaron Isaac was allowed, as the first Jew, to settle in Stockholm without converting. With the Dissenter Laws of 1860, it became permitted to leave the Church of Sweden, but only if you instead joined another state-approved community — the same period in which the free churches grew out of the revival movements. A decisive step was taken with the Freedom of Religion Act of 1951, which gave the right to stand entirely outside all faith communities. During the post-war period the country changed further through labour and refugee immigration, which brought Islam, Orthodox Christianity, Catholicism, Buddhism and Hinduism in greater numbers. In 1996 the rules were changed so that membership in the Church of Sweden followed from baptism rather than from birth, and on 1 January 2000 the church was separated from the state and became one faith community among others. Today, freedom of religion is protected in the Instrument of Government and the European Convention, while Sweden is strongly secularised — many people are not believers, but those who are have the right to practise their faith, and religion or other belief is one of the grounds in the Discrimination Act.
steps: The 16th and 17th centuries: after the Reformation, Sweden becomes Evangelical Lutheran, and the Uppsala Synod of 1593 establishes a single permitted doctrine.
The 18th and 19th centuries: individual exceptions emerge, including the right for Jews to settle from 1774–1775.
1860: the Dissenter Laws make it permitted to leave the Church of Sweden if you join another approved community — the free churches grow.
1951: the Freedom of Religion Act gives the right to stand entirely outside all faith communities.

1996 and 2000: membership is tied to baptism rather than birth, and on 1 January 2000 the Church of Sweden is separated from the state — today Sweden is marked by both secularisation and religious diversity.

questions.prompt: Summarise religion and society: freedom of religion, secularisation, state and church, religion in conflict and peace work, and prejudice and diversity.
questions.opener: The right first, then developments in Sweden and religion's role in the world.
questions.answer: Freedom of religion: protected in the Instrument of Government (a fundamental law), in the European Convention and in the UN's Universal Declaration, article 18 · positive side = the right to believe, practise and change religion · negative side = the right to stand outside · limitation: Swedish law applies equally to everyone, religious motives do not make a criminal act permitted · Secularisation: religion's declining influence over society's institutions and over many people's everyday lives · Sweden is counted as one of the world's most secularised countries, but many are still members of faith communities · State and church in Sweden: the Uppsala Synod of 1593 (a single doctrine) → Jewish settlement permitted 1774–1775 → the Dissenter Laws of 1860 (leaving allowed if you join another approved community) → the Freedom of Religion Act of 1951 (the right to stand entirely outside) → 1996 membership through baptism → 1 January 2000 the Church of Sweden is separated from the state · Religion in conflicts: conflicts usually have several causes — power, land, resources, identity — and religion can be used to motivate or reinforce them · Religion in peace work: mediation, aid work, reconciliation processes and interfaith dialogue · Prejudice: a preconceived view of a person or group without grounding in knowledge · can lead to discrimination and hate crime, e.g. Islamophobia and antisemitism · countered by knowledge, encounters and self-examination · Diversity in Sweden: the Church of Sweden and free churches, Islam, Orthodox Christianity, Catholicism, Judaism, Buddhism, Hinduism, and non-religious world views such as secular humanism · religion or other belief is one of the grounds of discrimination in the Discrimination Act.

questions.prompt: Which law from 1860 made it possible to leave the Church of Sweden, if you joined another approved faith community at the same time?
questions.opener: The word in the law's name refers to someone who deviates from the established doctrine.
choices: The Freedom of Religion Act of 1951
The Instrument of Government
The Discrimination Act
The Dissenter Laws
questions.explanation: The Dissenter Laws of 1860 made it possible to leave the Church of Sweden, but only if you joined another, state-approved faith community at the same time. The Freedom of Religion Act of 1951 went further and gave the right to stand entirely outside all faith communities, while the Instrument of Government and the Discrimination Act are other types of legislation.

questions.prompt: In which year was the Swedish Freedom of Religion Act adopted, giving the right to stand entirely outside all faith communities?
questions.opener: The year falls in the middle of the 1900s, after the Second World War.
questions.explanation: The Freedom of Religion Act of 1951 gave Swedish citizens the right to stand entirely outside all faith communities, a step further than the Dissenter Laws of 1860. The year 2000 is instead when the Church of Sweden was separated from the state, and 1774 is when Aaron Isaac was allowed to settle as a Jew in Sweden.

questions.prompt: What is prejudice and hatred directed specifically at Muslims called?
choices: Antisemitism
Secularisation
Diaspora
Islamophobia
questions.explanation: Islamophobia is the word for prejudice, fear and hatred directed specifically at Muslims or Islam. Antisemitism is instead directed at Jews, secularisation concerns religion's declining role in society, and diaspora refers to a people living scattered outside their historical homeland.

questions.prompt: What is prejudice and hatred directed specifically at Jews called?
questions.opener: The word has roots in an older term for Semitic peoples and languages.
choices: Islamophobia
Atheism
Agnosticism
Antisemitism
questions.explanation: Antisemitism is the word for prejudice, hatred and discrimination directed specifically at Jews. Islamophobia is instead directed at Muslims, while atheism and agnosticism are positions on belief in god, not forms of prejudice against a group.

questions.topic: religion in conflict and peace work
questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of religious actors working for peace?
questions.opener: Think about what's needed for warring parties to be able to approach each other again.
choices: Always financing armed groups
Refusing all contact with other religions
Never taking part in humanitarian aid work
Mediation and reconciliation processes between warring parties
questions.explanation: Religious leaders and organisations often work for peace through mediation, reconciliation processes and interfaith dialogue, as well as through humanitarian aid work in conflict-affected areas. Financing armed groups, refusing all contact with other religions, or avoiding aid work are, on the contrary, examples of how religion can help reinforce conflicts rather than resolve them.

questions.prompt: What is Sweden usually counted as in international comparisons regarding religion?
questions.opener: Think about how large a role religion plays in public life compared with many other countries.
choices: One of the world's most religious countries
A country with no freedom of religion at all
A country with a single permitted religion
One of the world's most secularised countries
questions.explanation: In international surveys, Sweden is often counted as one of the world's most secularised countries, where religion plays a less prominent role in public life and, for many people, in everyday life. Sweden also has freedom of religion enshrined in its constitution, so the claims about a lack of freedom of religion or a single permitted religion are not correct.

questions.prompt: What happened to the responsibility for civil registration in Sweden, which had previously belonged to the Church of Sweden?
questions.opener: The change happened a few years before the church was fully separated from the state.
choices: It still belongs to the Church of Sweden today
It was abolished entirely and no one keeps records any longer
It was moved to the UN
It was moved to the state (the Swedish Tax Agency) already in 1991, before the church was separated from the state in 2000
questions.explanation: Responsibility for civil registration was moved from the Church of Sweden to the state as early as 1991, a few years before the church was formally separated from the state on 1 January 2000. It is therefore not true that the responsibility remains with the church, that it was abolished entirely, or that it was moved to the UN.
